course_description: Global Histories of Architecture equips students to understand the nature of architecture by comparing through key moments and examples of architecture's global histories. The course looks at examples of architects responding to shifts in society, technology and geo-politics across a variety of cultures and times.

course_aims: This course equips students to understand the nature of architecture by comparing through key moments and examples of architecture's global histories.

learning_outcomes.description: Recognise the global nature of architecture in relation to historical shifts in society, culture, technology and geo-politics.
Recognise how the architectures of different cultures have evolved up to Modernism.
Develop critical skills in interpreting historical architecture through various theoretical frameworks.
Independently identify, select and synthetise information in written forms.
Recognise and use library systems and digital research technologies.

assessment_details.task_description: Assessment Rationale The practicals facilitate active engagement with course content during certain periods of workshop and provide an opportunity to engage with both primary and secondary sources on the historical periods covered in the Lecture parts of each week. They also build knowledge and skills in preparation for the Essay Assessment, including skills in research, analytical reading, precise writing, understanding scholarly arguments, appropriate utilisation of AI, and correct referencing practices, alongside learning the content for the end of the semester exam. The Tutorial Activities (Weeks 2-5) are progressive assessments and students should undertake the activities during the workshops. Each activity requires students to attend sessions in person, having done the required reading, be prepared to participate in a discussion and undertake the task. You can polish your work outside of the contact time prior to submission. Practical activities are an opportunity for peer-to-peer learning, but all submissions are individual work. Complex/Authentic assessment using AI and/or MT to support learning: This task has been designed to be challenging, authentic and complex. Whilst students may use AI and/or MT technologies, successful completion of assessment in this course will require students to critically engage in specific contexts and tasks for which artificial intelligence will provide only limited support and guidance. A failure to reference generative AI or MT use may constitute student misconduct under the Student Code of Conduct. To pass this assessment, students will be required to demonstrate detailed comprehension of their submission independent of AI and MT tools. Read full task description Hide full task description
assessment_details.assessment_security: Open assessment: In this assessment you can use resources such as your notes, course materials, and other tools, including AI, while completing the task. The focus is not on memorising information, but on understanding, applying judgement, and demonstrating your own thinking.
assessment_details.submission_guidelines:
The School of Architecture, Design and Planning uses Blackboard and Turnitin for assessment submission. Turnitin is accessed through the course Blackboard site. Turnitin also checks for plagiarism or instances where the original work of others is not appropriately acknowledged. Uploaded files must contain readable text and not be rasterised. Uploaded files must contain readable text and not be rasterised. Students are advised to commence assignment uploads with sufficient amount of time (consider possible technical problems with computers, internet speed, etc). After successfully submitting an assignment through Turnitin, a ‘Submission Complete!’ screen will be displayed. It is the student’s responsibility to check assignment preview and confirm successful submission. If the ‘Submission Complete!’ screen isn’t displayed, the student should regard the submission as unsuccessful. Students should download a copy of the digital receipt as proof they have submitted the assignment. Students who are experiencing upload issues must advise the Course Coordinator immediately by email and should include screenshots and a copy of the assessment for submission. To meet professional accreditation, public engagement and quality assurance obligations, digital copies of all course assessment items must be submitted in addition to any hard copy submission requirements specified in individual Course / Studio Outlines. Any physical models should be photographed and a minimum of two photographs describing the complete and full model must be included in the digital submission.
Deferral or extension
You may be able to apply for an extension .
The maximum extension allowed is 28 days. Extensions are given in multiples of 24 hours.
If a student wishes to apply for an extension, they must apply online on or before the assignment due date. When possible, it is suggested that requests are submitted 2 business days prior to the submission due date for the assignment to allow processing time. Students with outstanding applications for extensions are advised to submit their assessment by the original due date, irrespective of whether the work is complete, so that what has been done can be graded.
In the case students miss more than 1 weekly submission(s), a mark of 0 will be applied for that submission. This has been approved by the Associate Dean (Academic).
Late submission
The late penalty for this assessment item will be calculated as follows:
Standard 10% (or 1 grade) per day for 7 days

assessment_details.title: A2a: Referencing and Research Essay
assessment_details.task_description: Assessment Rationale: Students will write a 1000-word essay based on a self-selected architectural case study by following the rules and principles of referencing introduced in the course. The essay will draw on the themes, concepts, historical periods, buildings, texts and visual materials introduced in the course up to the point of submission. Students will respond to 2 out of 4 questions provided in the assessment task sheet. These questions will require students to interpret their selected case study in relation to broader architectural, historical, social and/or cultural contexts. The essay should develop a clear and focused argument in response to the selected questions. It is expected that students will support their discussion through appropriate references to course materials, scholarly sources and, where relevant, visual material such as photographs, drawings, plans, diagrams or other architectural representations. Students are also required to demonstrate appropriate source management by adding selected sources and relevant research materials to the nominated source management tool, which will be checked as part of the assessment process. assessment_details.title: A2b: Quiz
assessment_details.task_description: Assessment Rationale: An in-class quiz worth 10% will take place in Week 11 during workshop time. The quiz will assess students’ understanding of referencing, citation practices, source use and the correct application of the nominated referencing style. It will focus on skills introduced and practised in the course, including how to use sources responsibly, how to acknowledge ideas and evidence, and how to make scholarly work accountable through accurate referencing. In-person assessment prohibits use of AI or MT: This assessment task is to be completed in-person. The use of generative Artificial Intelligence (AI) or Machine Translation (MT) tools will not be permitted. Any attempted use of AI or MT may constitute student misconduct under the Student Code of Conduct. Read full task description Hide full task description

assessment_details.title: Final Exam
assessment_details.task_description: Assessment Rationale The final exam consists of three parts: Part 1: 10 multiple-choice questions (10 marks) — assesses students’ understanding of key terminology, concepts, buildings, periods, themes and ideas discussed in the course lectures and tutorials. The answer choices may be more developed than single-word responses and may require students to apply analytical judgement rather than simply recall information. Part 2: 3 short-answer questions (15 marks) — assesses students’ ability to interpret architectural, visual, historical and/or cultural material and relate it to key issues discussed in the lectures and tutorials. Each question is worth 5 marks. Part 3: Extended response question (15 marks) — assesses students’ ability to reflect on broader topics discussed in the lectures, tutorials and/or selected readings, and to connect their understanding of architectural history to relevant historical, social, cultural and/or spatial contexts. In-person assessment prohibits use of AI or MT: This assessment task is to be completed in-person. The use of generative Artificial Intelligence (AI) or Machine Translation (MT) tools will not be permitted. Any attempted use of AI or MT may constitute student misconduct under the Student Code of Conduct. Read full task description Hide full task description
